system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2173-08-26 20:57:00 to 2173-08-27 17:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with recurrent abdominal pain centered at the G-tube site and epigastric region, worsening after a recent G-tube exchange in clinic. Initial evaluation revealed no infection, obstruction, or perforation on imaging. CT showed ill-defined inflammatory changes around the G-tube insertion site without abscess. Pain was managed with oxycodone, and tube feeds were continued to prevent hypoglycemia. The patient developed asymptomatic hypotension, likely due to atenolol and pain-related hypovolemia, prompting discontinuation of atenolol to avoid masking hypoglycemia symptoms. Pain improved during the stay, and the patient was discharged home with a two-week supply of oxycodone, instructions to follow up with pain management and GI for EGD, and advised to discontinue atenolol permanently.
problems: Chronic gastrojejunal ulcer without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction

Dear Ms. ___,

You were admitted to ___ with 
increasing pain at your G-tube site. You were given oral 
Dilaudid with good effect. While you were here, we trialed bolus 
tube feedings, but unfortunately you could not tolerate them. 
Therefore, we will send you home on continuous tube feeds 
(NutriHep @ 50 cc/hour). Please continue to monitor your blood 
sugars when you return home.

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:

*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.

*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.

*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.

*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.

*You see blood or dark/black material when you vomit or have a 
bowel movement.

*You experience burning when you urinate, have blood in your 
urine, or experience a discharge.

*Your pain in not improving within ___ hours or is not gone 
within 24 hours. Call or return immediately if your pain is 
getting worse or changes location or moving to your chest or 
back.

*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.

*Any change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that concern 
you.

Please resume all regular home medications, unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.

Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids.

Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking pain 
medications.

Please follow up with your surgeon Dr. ___ at the 
appointment listed below.

Best wishes,
Your ___ surgical team

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team doctors. I understand you’re here because of increasing pain at your G-tube site. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse over the last few days. It’s a deep, constant ache right where the tube comes out. I was in the pain clinic yesterday, and they said it might be inflammation from the tube itself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what we’re seeing. Your CT scan shows some inflammation in the muscle around the tube, but no abscess or infection. We’ve seen this before—it’s a reaction to the presence of the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I already had the tube changed recently, and it didn’t help. Why is it still hurting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes the tissue becomes sensitized, and even a new tube can cause irritation. We tried injecting a steroid through the tube earlier, but you didn’t get much relief, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, it only helped a little for a few hours. Is there anything else we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we’re focusing on pain control. We’ve switched you from oxycodone to dilaudid by mouth, which seems to be working better. How’s the pain now, on a scale from 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s about a 5 now. That’s much better than earlier—thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that going as needed. You’re still on continuous tube feeds at 40 cc/hr, and we tried giving a bolus earlier, but your blood sugar dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I felt shaky and weak. I’ve had that before—my hypoglycemia kicks in fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’ve gone back to continuous feeds to keep your sugars stable. We’ll send you home on NutriHep at 50 cc/hour. You’ll need to keep checking your blood sugar regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. But what about the tube? The pain clinic said it might need to be removed or replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s something to discuss with your surgeon. Right now, removing it isn’t urgent since there’s no infection. But if the pain continues, we may need to consider it. For now, we’re managing the inflammation and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night well—vitals are stable, no fever, and your pain has been controlled. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Will I still have the pain at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have dilaudid to take as needed every 4 hours. If the pain isn’t improving within a day or gets worse, please call your surgeon or come back. Also, watch for fever, redness, or drainage at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll keep the feeds going continuously and check my sugars?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Continue all your regular medications too, unless told otherwise. You have a follow-up with your surgeon soon—we’ll go over next steps then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Just take it easy, stay hydrated, and don’t drive while on the pain meds. We’ll get your discharge papers ready shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—we reviewed your discharge instructions. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, everything’s clear. I’ll follow up with my surgeon and keep an eye on my symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your prescriptions and discharge paperwork now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when she is.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with worsening pain at her G-tube site, persistent despite a recent tube exchange and prior steroid injection. Imaging showed inflammatory changes around the tube without abscess or infection. Pain was initially managed with oxycodone but transitioned to oral hydromorphone (dilaudid) with improved control. A trial of bolus tube feeds was unsuccessful due to hypoglycemia, so she was maintained on continuous feeds. The patient remained stable, afebrile, and hemodynamically normal throughout the stay. She was discharged home on continuous tube feeds (NutriHep at 50 cc/hr), dilaudid for breakthrough pain, and instructions to monitor blood glucose and follow up with her surgeon.
